turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Howzit sir. I've just done your blood pressure, it's 148 over 86, and your pulse is 74. You can head in, the doctor's ready.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, thanks hey. These waiting room magazines are from last year, I swear. My wife is parking the bakkie, the robot on Main was stuck.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in, come in. She can join us when she gets here. Howzit, what's been bothering you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the nights, doc. I'm getting up to pass water three or four times, the stream is weak, and it dribbles after. I'm properly tired of it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late. I had to collect my Metformine at the chemist, those are my sugar tablets, and then the parking was full.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're here, that's what counts. Tell me more about this passing water business.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, umm, when it started I can't really say. Before Christmas, or was it the winter? A good few months anyway, and my mate at bowls has the same story and talks my ear off.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Three or four times is rough on your sleep. Is it hard to get the stream going as well?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I stand there and wait. Then it's slow, and at the end it dribbles. Saturday at the braai I had to sneak off behind the garage, and the guys thought that was hilarious.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I hear the toilet three times, easy. The passage light goes on and that's me awake too.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine at all? Even once?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood. It looks normal, yellow, darker like strong tea if I've been in the garden and not drinking.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Speaking of tea, what are you drinking in the evenings?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Rooibos. Two cups, sometimes three, after supper, while the rugby is on. I gave up night coffee ages ago, and there's a glass of water next to the bed, old habit.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): That late fluid will nudge the bladder. Any pain or burning when you pass water?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. It's more the standing and waiting than an actual pain.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): And in the daytime, are you rushing for the toilet, or leaking on your clothes?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not rushing really. Not wet through the day either, just that little dribble at the end. I still drive out to the co-op fine. They had mielie meal on special, two bags for the price of one.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ha, save me the specials. How are the bowels? Any constipation?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Of. No. Bowels are fine, nice and regular. She makes pap and vegetables and I eat what's put down.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does, most nights. Except when there are koeksisters, then the diet goes out the window.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Which medicines are you taking now?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. For the pressure I take Mizartan, eighty milligrams, one in the morning. And Omprazole for the acid, twenty milligrams, also in the morning, the little capsule from the chemist.
[SEG0024] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He forgets the Omprazole some mornings, especially if we leave early for the market.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, not always. Maybe once or twice a week I skip it when we're rushing. The Mizartan I have with breakfast, that one I don't miss.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the acid one is hit and miss, and the pressure one is steady. Any allergies, medicines or foods, anything that swells you up?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. You can give me whatever.
[SEG0028] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hold on. Didn't your face swell with that antibiotic after the tooth? Years ago, you were puffy.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know if it was the tablet or the tooth. I don't count it. It was ages ago and nobody wrote it down.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we'll leave it as a possible reaction to an antibiotic, not confirmed. I'd rather not use that family of medicine on you. Now, diabetes, heart problems, anything longstanding?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The pressure is the one, it's been years. Heartburn comes and goes, that's why the Omprazole. No diabetes, that's my wife's thing, not me. My father had prostate trouble and they did an operation when he was old, but me I still mow the lawn, slowly.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you had any operation yourself? Prostate, hernia, appendix?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never been cut. Appendix is still in, knock on wood.
[SEG0034] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Only a tooth pulled. That's not an operation, hey.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not the same thing, no. Do you smoke, or drink?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped the smokes when my daughter was born, that's twenty years now. Alcohol is a brandy on a Friday if someone braais, not every week. Mornings I walk the dog round the block. He's a staffie called Biltong, mad as a snake.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good life. Let me examine you. Your tummy is soft, no masses, and the bladder doesn't feel full. On the finger exam the prostate is smoothly enlarged, not hard, and I don't feel nodules.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Eish, warn a man. My neighbour reckons that exam is worse than traffic fines. So is it cancer? I think my father's was, but they never said the word out loud.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't say cancer from what I feel. It fits an enlarged prostate that feels benign, and that lines up with the weak stream, the dribble and waking at night. I'm arranging a PSA blood test and a urine test, both today.
[SEG0040] person_1 (NURSE): Urine bottle is on the side, and I'll print the PSA blood form. The lab down the passage is open till four.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll give it a go. Don't expect a firehose, hey.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): For the symptoms I'm going to start tamsulosin, 0.4 milligrams, one capsule at night. It relaxes things at the prostate so the stream can improve. Your pressure can dip with it, so you may feel dizzy standing up. Get up slowly.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Night time capsule, ok. Will the waking actually stop? And must I give up the rooibos, because Biltong still wants his walk even if I'm dizzy.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep the rooibos if it makes you happy, maybe move one cup to before supper and we'll see if the nights ease. If you get very dizzy, or you cannot pass water at all, come back sooner, don't sit on it.
[SEG0045] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll keep an eye on him when he stands up. Doctor, my sister takes biotin for her hair and she swears by it. Would that help his bladder at all?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Biotin is hers, it won't touch the waterworks. We'll stick with the tamsulosin. And the follow-up is in six weeks, that's booked with reception.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, sharp. Umm, my knees are stiff in the mornings, old rugby knees, but that's not why I came. Oh, and the Mizartan won't fight with this new capsule? Eighty milligrams, mornings, like I said.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Knees we can park for another visit if they grumble. Mizartan in the morning and tamsulosin at night, they can both soften the pressure a little, but there's no clash that stops us. That's the slow standing again.
[SEG0049] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had a urine test last year at the GP and they said it was fine. Do we still need another?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, I still want a fresh urine today. Last year doesn't tell me about this week. The nurse has the bottle, and the PSA form.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): Bottle's there, and the PSA form is printing. Bloods close at four, so don't stop for coffee. Reception will hand you the six week card on the way out.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Four o'clock, ja. If the bakkie starts we're laughing. It was sulking this morning, needs a new battery I reckon.
[SEG0053] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It'll start. I drove it here. Come, before you tell the doctor about the tyres as well.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Go well. Urine first, then the bloods, and the tamsulosin from the chemist tonight. See you in six weeks.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Patient denies allergies, but transcript also notes possible unconfirmed antibiotic reaction.

omissions.text: Patient reports being tired from the nocturia/disturbed sleep.
Dysuria was asked about and essentially denied as pain/burning: patient said 'sometimes, not really' and that it is more standing and waiting than actual pain.
Omeprazole adherence detail: patient forgets/skips it once or twice a week, especially when leaving early; Mizartan adherence is steady and he does not miss it.
Possible antibiotic reaction was not just disputed by family; doctor documented it clinically as a possible unconfirmed antibiotic reaction and said he would rather avoid that family of medicine.
Heart problems were specifically asked about and denied by the patient.
Past surgical history detail: specifically denied prior prostate surgery, hernia surgery, and appendix surgery ('never been cut').

Family history detail may be understated/wrongly generalized: patient said his father had prostate trouble and had an operation when old; he also expressed uncertainty that it might have been cancer, but this was not confirmed.
Doctor counselled that tamsulosin may improve the stream by relaxing the prostate/outlet.
Red-flag advice included to come back sooner if he cannot pass urine at all, specifically 'don't sit on it'.

Question about interaction was answered: Mizartan in the morning and tamsulosin at night can both lower blood pressure a little, but there is no contraindicating interaction/clash preventing use together.
Prior investigation history: family member said he had a urine test last year at the GP and it was fine; doctor still wanted a fresh urine test today because last year does not reflect this week.

Urinary pain/burning was not clearly absent; patient gave an equivocal answer ('Sometimes, not really. It's more the standing and waiting than an actual pain'), so recording it as a definite negative is inaccurate.
